# Random Forest for Classification

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical foundations of bootstrap sampling, ensembles, and Random Forest are developed in Chapters 7 and 14 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to explain how Random Forest combines many decision trees, interpret the role of bootstrap samples and random predictor selection, fit a model in R, examine variable importance, and evaluate performance on held-out data.

## Core idea

A Random Forest combines many partially different decision trees. For classification, the final prediction is typically obtained by majority vote:

$$
\hat{y}(x)=\operatorname{mode}\left\{\hat{y}^{(1)}(x),\hat{y}^{(2)}(x),\ldots,\hat{y}^{(B)}(x)\right\}.
$$

Each tree is built from a bootstrap sample and considers only a random subset of predictors at each split. These two sources of randomness reduce correlation among trees and usually improve stability relative to a single tree.

## Out-of-bag error

Observations not selected in a particular bootstrap sample are called *out-of-bag* (OOB) observations for that tree. They can be used to obtain an internal estimate of predictive error without fitting a separate model for each resample.

::: {.callout-note title="OOB is useful, but the final test set still matters"}
OOB error is valuable for model development, but a final untouched test set remains the clearest estimate of out-of-sample performance when one has been reserved.
:::

## ATUS example

The Spanish edition fits a probabilistic Random Forest with `ranger`, using month, hour, day of week, accident type, and cause to classify accidents as **with victims** or **property damage only**.

The workflow separates training and test data before fitting the forest and evaluates the resulting class predictions with a confusion matrix, sensitivity, and specificity.

## Variable importance

Random Forest can report different forms of variable importance. Impurity-based importance measures how much a predictor contributes to impurity reduction across trees.

::: {.callout-warning title="Importance is not causality"}
A high importance score means that a variable was useful for prediction in this fitted model. It does not establish a causal relationship with the outcome and may be affected by predictor scale, cardinality, correlation, and the chosen importance measure.
:::

For stronger interpretation, permutation importance is often preferable when computationally feasible because it evaluates how predictive performance changes after disrupting one predictor.

## COVID-19 educational route

The processed COVID-19 dataset should be selected dynamically instead of fixing a calendar year in the source code.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ranger)

files_covid <- list.files(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  pattern = "covid19_mexico_[0-9]{4}_ml_preparado\\.csv\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

if (length(files_covid) == 0) {
  stop("No prepared COVID-19 data file was found.")
}

covid_rf <- read_csv(files_covid[1], show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```

A training/test split can then be created and the model fitted with `ranger(..., probability = TRUE)`.

## Probabilities and class decisions

A probabilistic forest returns estimated class probabilities. Converting those probabilities to labels requires a threshold or another decision rule.

As in logistic regression, discrimination and calibration should not be confused. Good ranking of observations does not guarantee well-calibrated probabilities.

::: {.callout-important title="Sampling affects probability interpretation"}
If the educational COVID-19 sample was balanced or enriched with deaths, the raw class probabilities produced by the forest should not be interpreted as population risk without appropriate weighting or recalibration.
:::

## Comparing a tree with a forest

A single decision tree is usually easier to explain, while a Random Forest is often more stable and more accurate because it averages many different trees. The trade-off is reduced transparency at the level of individual decision rules.

## Educational and ethical note

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
The COVID-19 model in this chapter is designed to teach ensemble classification. It is not a medical diagnostic system, a clinical prognostic model, or a decision-support tool.
:::

## Chapter summary

Random Forest improves the stability of individual trees by combining bootstrap sampling, random predictor selection, and aggregation. Its strengths include strong predictive performance and robustness; its limitations include reduced interpretability and the need for careful interpretation of variable importance and predicted probabilities.
